domains.title: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration
domains.sub: Designing agent loops, coordinators and subagents, hooks, and sessions.

lessons.title: Agentic Loops
lessons.tests: how a loop decides to continue or stop, and why `stop_reason` beats text parsing or iteration caps.
rules: Continue on `stop_reason: "tool_use"`, stop on `"end_turn"`. The exam tests only these two values.
Reject all three anti-patterns: parsing "I'm done" text, iteration caps as primary control, checking for text content as completion.
Model-driven tool selection is favoured, except where deterministic compliance needs code enforcement.
traps: Checking `content[0].type == "text"` for completion
text can accompany tool_use; use `stop_reason`.
Iteration cap to fix premature termination
caps stop runaway loops, not early exits; fix the `stop_reason` check. Caps are only a safety net.
Parsing natural-language "task complete"
ambiguous; use `stop_reason`.
Dropping tool results or swapping history for a summary to save tokens
API is stateless; append every result, shrink large results at the tool.

lessons.title: Multi-Agent Orchestration
lessons.tests: the hub-and-spoke coordinator pattern, subagent isolation, and tracing coverage gaps back to the coordinator.
rules: Only hub-and-spoke is tested: coordinator at the centre, all four coordinator responsibilities.
Direct subagent-to-subagent communication is always wrong on the exam, even if framed as "more efficient".
Sample Q7: coordinator splits "AI in creative industries" into only visual arts → root cause is the coordinator's decomposition.
Forks (copy full coordinator context) exist in current product, but the exam tests the isolation rule.
traps: Blaming subagents for coverage gaps
coordinator's decomposition was too narrow.
Assuming subagents share memory/history
they get only what the coordinator puts in the prompt.
Direct inter-subagent messaging
bypasses observability and error handling; route via coordinator.
Running every query through all subagents (even with caching)
coordinator invokes only the subagents needed.

lessons.title: Subagent Invocation and Context Passing
lessons.tests: what context a subagent receives, passing structured metadata, parallel spawning, and resume vs fork.
rules: Answer "Task tool" (exam name), even though current code says Agent.
Unsourced claims in a synthesis report → coordinator passed content without structured metadata.
Independent subtasks → parallel spawn; look for "in a single response" / "simultaneously".
`--resume` continues a session; `fork_session` branches from it.
traps: Assuming subagents inherit coordinator history
isolated; pass everything explicitly.
Blaming the synthesis prompt for lost citations
pass findings as structured data with URL, doc name, page.
Sequential invocation of independent tasks
multiple Task calls in one coordinator response.
Rigid step-by-step subagent prompts
state the goal and quality criteria, let it choose how.

lessons.title: Workflow Enforcement and Handoff
lessons.tests: when to use programmatic enforcement over prompts, prerequisite gates, and complete human handoffs.
rules: Most-repeated rule: prompt guidance vs programmatic enforcement. Money/security/compliance → always programmatic.
Compound requests: decompose, investigate in parallel with shared context, reply once.
traps: Stronger system prompt or few-shot for high-stakes compliance
still probabilistic; use programmatic enforcement.
Handling multi-concern requests one at a time
decompose, parallelise, one unified resolution.
Routing classifier to fix in-agent compliance
failure is in the execution sequence; add a prerequisite gate.
Handoff summary missing fields
must be self-contained: customer ID, summary, root cause, refund amount, recommended action.

lessons.title: Agent SDK Hooks
lessons.tests: when PreToolUse and PostToolUse fire, and which one blocks actions vs transforms results.
rules: Know when each hook fires. For a 100% requirement, the answer is a hook.
traps: PostToolUse to block violations
action already happened; use PreToolUse.
Prompt instructions for 100% compliance
hooks give the deterministic guarantee.
Letting the model normalise mixed tool data formats
PostToolUse hook normalises before the model sees it.
PreToolUse to clean tool results
it sees the outgoing call, not the result; use PostToolUse.

lessons.title: Task Decomposition Strategies
lessons.tests: choosing fixed pipelines vs dynamic decomposition, and fixing attention dilution with per-item passes.
rules: Match pattern to task: fixed pipeline for known steps, dynamic adaptive decomposition for open-ended investigation.
14-file single-pass review with declining quality → 14 per-file passes + 1 cross-file integration pass.
traps: Better model / larger context / more detailed prompt for attention dilution
split into per-item passes + integration pass.
Dynamic decomposition for a structured, known task
fixed pipeline is more predictable.
Fixed pipeline for open-ended investigation
needs adaptive decomposition.
Batching files without a cross-file pass
misses cross-batch data flow and inconsistencies.

lessons.title: Session State and Resumption
lessons.tests: when to resume a session, when to start fresh with a summary, and stale tool results.
rules: Prior context mostly valid → resume. Tool results stale → fresh session + injected structured summary.
Typical Q: resumed after files changed, agent contradicts itself → fresh session + summary + targeted re-analysis of changed files.
traps: Full re-exploration of 50 files when 3 changed
tell the agent which 3 changed.
Resuming when most tool results are stale
start fresh with summary.
`fork_session` to continue one line of work
use `--resume`; fork is for comparing approaches.
`fork_session` to fix stale context
fork inherits the stale context.

domains.title: Tool Design & MCP Integration
domains.sub: Writing tool descriptions, error responses, tool scoping, and MCP setup.

lessons.title: Tool Interface Design
lessons.tests: fixing tool misrouting with better descriptions first, and when the toolset itself is the problem.
rules: Sample Q2 (`get_customer` vs `lookup_order` misrouting): fix = expand descriptions. Few-shot, routing classifier and consolidation are wrong as first steps.
Exam pattern: low-effort, high-impact first. Descriptions before classifiers, scoped before full access, community servers before custom.
Descriptions fix a workable set where two tools look alike; they don't fix a too-large toolset (guide example: 18 tools vs 4 to 5).
Splitting example: `analyze_document` → `extract_data_points`, `summarize_content`, `verify_claim_against_source`.
traps: Few-shot to fix misrouting
token cost, doesn't fix root cause; fix descriptions.
Routing classifier first
over-engineered, bypasses the LLM.
Consolidating tools first
valid long-term, too much effort as step one.
Ignoring system prompt after fixing descriptions
keyword wording in the system prompt can override; review it.

lessons.title: Structured Error Responses
lessons.tests: access failures vs valid empty results, the four error categories, and the `isRetryable` flag.
rules: Key distinction: access failure vs valid empty result.
Know the four error categories and `isRetryable` by name. Ask: would resending this exact call work?
traps: Retrying an empty successful query
that is the answer; accept it.
Generic "Operation failed"
include `errorCategory`, `isRetryable`, description.
Business errors (refund over limit) as retryable
never resolve by retry; escalate.
Validation error marked `isRetryable: true`
false; the input must change first.
Reading `isRetryable: false` as "abandon"
recover via corrected input, alternative path or escalation.
Subagent returning empty-as-success on error
return structured error context (type, query, partial results).

lessons.title: Tool Distribution & Tool Choice
lessons.tests: how many tools each agent should hold, scoped cross-role tools, and `tool_choice` modes.
rules: "18 vs 4 to 5 tools per agent" is illustrative, not a hard limit. Use that framing on the exam (current docs say 30 to 50).
Consolidation and constraint can both be right in one system.
Sample Q9: 85% of verifications are simple → give synthesis agent a scoped `verify_fact` tool; complex 15% still via coordinator (least privilege).
traps: Routing all simple lookups via coordinator
scoped cross-role tool cuts hops and latency.
`tool_choice: "auto"` when structured output is required
exam answer is `"any"` (or forced tool).
18 tools on one agent
split by role into small sets.
Generic `fetch_url` for documents
constrained `load_document` (least privilege).

lessons.title: MCP Server Integration
lessons.tests: community vs custom MCP servers, project vs user config scope, and keeping secrets out of git.
rules: Standard integration → "evaluate community servers first" is always right. Build custom only for explicit team-specific needs.
Project `.mcp.json` = shared, version-controlled. User `~/.claude.json` = personal. Use `${ENV_VAR}` for credentials.
traps: Custom server for Jira
use a community server.
Team config in `~/.claude.json`
goes in project `.mcp.json`.
Token pasted in `.mcp.json` because repo is private
use `${GITHUB_TOKEN}`.
System prompt rule or removing built-ins to force MCP tool use
expand the MCP tool's description.

lessons.title: Built-in Tools
lessons.tests: picking the right built-in tool (Grep vs Glob, Edit vs Read + Write) and exploring incrementally.
rules: Grep = file contents. Glob = file paths. This distinction matters most.
Edit first; Read + Write only when Edit can't find a unique anchor. Never read all files upfront.
Deprecation question: Grep → Glob → Grep again for wrapped/renamed callers. Starting with Glob is wrong.
Treat Grep and Glob as built-in tools on the exam.
traps: Glob to find function callers
Grep.
Grep to find files by name pattern
Glob.
Reading all source files upfront
Grep for entry points, then Read incrementally.
Read + Write by default
Edit first.
Widening `old_string` / `replace_all` on non-unique match
exam answer is Read + Write.

domains.title: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
domains.sub: CLAUDE.md levels, skills, path rules, plan mode, refinement, and CI/CD.

lessons.title: CLAUDE.md Hierarchy
lessons.tests: which CLAUDE.md level applies where, and diagnosing config stored at the wrong level.
rules: Favourite trap: "new team member" + "inconsistent behaviour" → conventions sit in user-level `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`; move to project level.
Answer `/memory` as the command that shows loaded files (exam guide), though `/context` is the real-world one.
traps: New teammate missing instructions
move from `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` to `.claude/CLAUDE.md`.
Thinking `/memory` triggers loading
it's diagnostic only; loading follows the hierarchy.
Directory-level CLAUDE.md for cross-directory conventions
`.claude/rules/` with glob paths.

lessons.title: Custom Slash Commands and Skills
lessons.tests: skills vs CLAUDE.md, correct file paths and scope, frontmatter options, and `context: fork`.
rules: On-demand workflow (skill) vs persistent config (CLAUDE.md / rules).
Verbose output cluttering main chat → `context: fork`.
Three frontmatter options tested; answer with guide wording: `allowed-tools` "restricts" tool access; `argument-hint` prompts for missing parameters.
traps: Flat `.claude/skills/review.md`
skill needs `.claude/skills/review/SKILL.md` (flat files go in `.claude/commands/`).
Team command in `~/.claude/...`
project-scoped path in the repo.
Skills for always-on guidance
use CLAUDE.md or rules.
Verbose skill running inline
`context: fork`.
Task workflows in CLAUDE.md
put them in skills.

lessons.title: Path-Specific Rules
lessons.tests: using `.claude/rules/` with glob paths for conventions spread across many directories.
rules: Co-located test files across many directories → always path-specific rules with glob patterns.
traps: CLAUDE.md in every directory
path rules instead.
File-type conventions in root CLAUDE.md
wastes tokens; path rules load only on matching files.
Skills vs rules for auto conventions
rules (they stay in context and shape every edit).

lessons.title: Plan Mode vs Direct Execution
lessons.tests: picking plan mode or direct execution for a task, and the plan-then-execute hybrid.
rules: Common right answer: hybrid. Plan mode first, then direct execution.
traps: Direct execution for multi-file architectural change
plan mode.
Plan mode for single-file fix with clear stack trace
direct execution.
Verbose discovery in main chat
Explore subagent.
Switching to plan mode only when complexity appears
if complexity is stated upfront, plan upfront.

lessons.title: Iterative Refinement Techniques
lessons.tests: which refinement technique to use first: examples, test-driven iteration, interview, or batched feedback.
rules: Prose interpreted inconsistently → 2 to 3 concrete input/output examples.
Complex transformation with many edge cases → test-driven iteration.
Unfamiliar domain → interview pattern.
Interacting issues → one batched message. Independent issues → sequential.
traps: More precise prose
examples instead.
Interacting fixes one at a time
send together.
Interview pattern when transformation is known
examples.

lessons.title: CI/CD Integration
lessons.tests: running Claude Code headless in CI (`-p`), independent review sessions, and batch vs real-time API.
rules: Most-tested D3 fact (sample Q10): CI job hangs waiting for input → `-p` flag. `CLAUDE_HEADLESS` and `--batch` don't exist.
Also tested: session isolation, headless flags, append vs replace, Batch API decision (sample Q11).
Reported: 4 to 5 questions on GitHub Actions; worktrees appear in practice questions.
traps: `CLAUDE_HEADLESS`, `--batch`, stdin redirect
Self-review in the same session
independent review instance.
Batch API for pre-merge checks
real-time API for blocking work; batch for overnight.
Reviewing only the new diff or resuming the old session to avoid repeats
fresh whole-PR run with previous findings passed in.

domains.title: Prompt Engineering & Structured Output
domains.sub: Explicit criteria, few-shot, structured output, retries, batch, and review.

lessons.title: System Prompts with Explicit Criteria
lessons.tests: replacing vague instructions with explicit criteria, and managing false positives by category.
rules: Vague instructions ("be conservative", "only high-confidence findings") are the classic wrong options.
False positives in one category reduce trust in every category.
traps: "Be conservative"
specific categorical criteria: what to flag, what to skip.
Confidence thresholds for false positives
explicit criteria with code examples first.
Keeping noisy categories on while fixing them
temporarily disable them.

lessons.title: Few-Shot Prompting
lessons.tests: when few-shot examples beat more instructions, and which other technique fits each output problem.
rules: Inconsistent output despite detailed instructions → add few-shot examples.

Technique map: formatting → few-shot · malformed JSON → tool_use + schema · fabricated values → nullable fields · wrong tool → descriptions first · missed narrative info → few-shot · sum mismatch → validation-retry loop.
traps: More instructions for inconsistent format
show examples.
Many examples for every case
2 to 4 targeted examples with reasoning (exam guide).
Confidence thresholds for inconsistent judgement
few-shot on ambiguous cases.

lessons.title: Structured Output with Tool Use
lessons.tests: `tool_choice` modes, what schemas do and don't prevent, and nullable vs required fields.
rules: Exam uses three `tool_choice` modes (auto / any / forced). Guaranteed structured output for unknown doc type → `"any"`.
Usual trap: believing tool_use prevents all extraction errors.
traps: tool_use prevents all errors
fixes syntax only, not semantic errors; validate separately.
`"auto"` to guarantee a tool call
`"any"` (exam answer).
All fields required
make possibly-missing fields nullable to avoid fabrication.

lessons.title: Validation, Retry, and Feedback Loops
lessons.tests: which extraction failures a retry can fix, and what a good retry request must include.
rules: Most tested: retry effectiveness boundary, meaning which failures are fixable by retry.
Retry request includes document + failed extraction + specific validation error.
traps: Retries always work
can't create info absent from the source; send to review or return null.
Retry without the specific error
include it (e.g., "items sum to £450, total says £500").
Source contradicts itself
extract both (`calculated_total`, `stated_total`, `conflict_detected`) and route to review.
Pydantic redundant with schema
schemas can't express cross-field rules; Pydantic does.

lessons.title: Batch Processing Strategies
lessons.tests: matching workflows to batch or synchronous APIs, the 24-hour window, and tool-call limits in batch.
rules: Sample Q11: keep blocking workflows synchronous; batch only latency-tolerant ones.
Batch can't run your own tool mid-request and continue → that step needs the synchronous API.
Scheduling questions may work back from an SLA to submission frequency.
traps: Everything to batch for savings
no latency SLA, up to 24h.
Assuming batch is usually fast
design for the 24h maximum.
Batch with mid-request client tool calls
run that step synchronously.

lessons.title: Multi-Instance and Multi-Pass Review
lessons.tests: independent review instances, multi-pass review for large changes, and calibrated confidence.
rules: Better review → separate model instance. Not "review carefully" in the same session, not extended thinking in that session.
Raw confidence = unreliable; calibrated thresholds (validated on labelled sets) = OK for routing.
traps: Same-session self-review
independent instance.
Single pass for large multi-file reviews
per-file passes + integration pass.
Larger context model for attention dilution
focused per-file passes.
Uncalibrated confidence for routing
calibrate on labelled sets first.

domains.title: Context Management & Reliability
domains.sub: Context windows, escalation, error handling, degradation, review, and provenance.

lessons.title: Context Window Management
lessons.tests: keeping key facts through summarisation, lost-in-the-middle fixes, and trimming tool results.
rules: Agent loses amounts/dates after summarisation → persistent case facts block.
Prompt caching: only its existence and purpose are tested.
traps: Progressive summarisation for transactional data
keep numbers/dates/IDs in a case facts block.
"Pay attention to everything" for lost-in-the-middle
key findings at the start + section headers.
Keeping full tool results "just in case"
trim to relevant fields.
Selective truncation of history
API is stateless; pass full history, use facts block + summarisation.

lessons.title: Escalation & Ambiguity Resolution
lessons.tests: valid vs unreliable escalation triggers, and how to handle ambiguous customer matches.
rules: Valid triggers: explicit human request (immediately), policy gaps, inability to progress.
Unreliable triggers: sentiment and self-reported confidence.
traps: Escalating on frustration
sentiment doesn't track complexity.
Self-reported confidence for escalation
explicit criteria + few-shot.
Trying to resolve before honouring "I want a human"
escalate in that reply.
Picking the most recent/active of ambiguous customer matches

lessons.title: Error Propagation in Multi-Agent Systems
lessons.tests: passing structured error context to the coordinator, and recovery without stopping the pipeline.
rules: Subagent timeout → subagent returns structured error context so the coordinator decides recovery.
Access failures may warrant retry; valid empty results never.
traps: Timeout returned as empty success
structured error (type, query, partial results, alternatives).
Terminating the whole pipeline on one timeout
targeted recovery, keep partial results.
Generic "search unavailable" after retries
structured error context.
Retrying a valid empty result
that is the answer.

lessons.title: Codebase Exploration & Context Degradation
lessons.tests: spotting context degradation, and fixing it with scratchpads, subagents and state manifests.
rules: Symptom: agent cites "typical patterns" instead of classes it found → scratchpad files.
Degradation is not a token problem. Subagents are mainly for isolation. Use `/compact` proactively.
Crash recovery → state manifest loaded on resume and injected into prompts (exam answer).
traps: Bigger context window
scratchpad file for key findings.
Expecting next-phase subagents to inherit history, or passing full transcripts
inject a summary of key findings.
Restarting without saving state
persist via scratchpad/manifest first.
`/compact` only at the limit
use it proactively.

lessons.title: Human Review & Confidence Calibration
lessons.tests: validating accuracy by segment, calibrating confidence, and allocating limited reviewer time.
rules: Wrong answers: trust aggregate accuracy, sample only low-confidence, raw scores, even reviewer spread.
97% overall can hide 40% error on one doc type → validate by doc type and field.
traps: Aggregate accuracy to automate
segment by type/field first.
Sampling only low-confidence items
stratified random sampling of high-confidence too.
Raw confidence scores
calibrate on labelled sets.
Even reviewer allocation
prioritise highest-uncertainty items.

lessons.title: Information Provenance & Multi-Source Synthesis
lessons.tests: keeping claim-source links through synthesis, handling conflicting sources, and matching format to content.
rules: Two credible conflicting values → annotate both with attribution and dates. Never pick most recent, average or most authoritative.
Map each claim to URL, document, excerpt, date, preserved through synthesis. Match format to content.
traps: Picking the most recent source
keep both, let the reader decide.
Treating different numbers as contradictions
dates often explain them; require dates.
Synthesis paraphrasing loses mappings
subagents emit structured claim-source data.
One format for everything
tables for financials, prose for news, lists for technical findings.

intro.metaLead: These patterns recur in lesson after lesson. When two options both look right, check them against these first.
metaRules: Start from the stated need, not the impressive option

When a scenario names a measured cost driver, constraint or requirement, the narrow option that targets it beats the broad, sophisticated one. Over-engineering is marked wrong as often as under-engineering.
A bigger model is almost never the first fix
Upgrading the model, raising the tier or loading more context is a favourite wrong answer. Find the failing stage first: prompt, retrieval, validation, configuration or feedback loop.
An instruction is not a control
A system prompt line or a shared instruction file shapes behaviour but enforces nothing. If something must never happen, remove or scope the capability, or enforce it in code or config.
Prevent where the requirement says never

Logging and periodic review detect harm after it happens. Confirmations and alerts compensate. When a role never needs a capability, or harm must never reach a user, the preventive answer wins: remove it or gate it before the action.
Evidence before change, and protect every fix
Read traces and correlate with recent changes before editing anything. Change one thing at a time, re-run evals in both directions, and turn each failure into a regression case.

Assuming subagents see the parent chat or each other

intro.metaLead: These five patterns decide most questions in every section. Learn them before the lessons.

Underline the deciding words: most cost-effective, least operational effort, no code changes, global, compliant. Two options usually work; only one meets that phrase.
Managed beats self-built.

Google's recommended practice wins.

Answer from the case study's requirements.

domains.title: Designing and Planning a Cloud Solution
domains.sub: Turn business and technical requirements into a design: the right compute, storage, network, AI service and recovery plan for the scenario.

lessons.title: Requirements, Trade-offs and Cost
lessons.tests: whether you can find the one requirement in a long scenario that decides the answer, and weigh cost against availability and effort.
rules: Business requirements say why (cut cost, move faster, meet a regulation); technical requirements say how (containers, private network, 99.9% uptime).
The deciding phrase is usually small: "most cost-effective", "least operational effort", "without changing code" or "globally".
Total cost of ownership includes people, licences, egress and missed-SLA penalties, not only the VM bill.
traps: The most available design is always the best answer
The cheapest design that still meets every stated requirement
Extra availability costs money. The exam rewards meeting the stated needs at the lowest cost, not going beyond them.
Multi-regional by default, just in case
Regional when the scenario only needs one region
Multi-region adds cost and complexity. If users and requirements sit in one region, a regional design spread across zones is enough.
Compare options on compute price alone
Compare total cost: operations staff, licences, network and downtime
Licences, staff time, network egress and outage penalties often outweigh the VM bill, so the cheaper VM can be the dearer solution.
Build a custom tool for a gap
A managed service that already does it, unless a requirement rules it out
A self-built tool is more code to run and maintain. Google's answer almost always prefers an existing managed service.

lessons.title: Choosing Compute
lessons.tests: which compute service fits the workload: Compute Engine, GKE Standard, GKE Autopilot, Cloud Run or App Engine.
rules: More control means more work: Compute Engine, then GKE Standard, GKE Autopilot, Cloud Run, Cloud Run functions.
Containers with spiky or unpredictable traffic and no cluster to run: Cloud Run, which scales to zero.
Kubernetes but no node management: GKE Autopilot, billed on Pod requests. Need GPUs, special nodes or node access: GKE Standard.
traps: GKE for a single stateless container API
Cloud Run: no cluster, scales to zero
A cluster brings node, upgrade and networking work you don't need for one stateless service. Cloud Run runs the same container with none of it.
Compute Engine for a lift-and-shift of containerised apps with minimal effort
Cloud Run (or GKE if they already run Kubernetes)
Containers on plain VMs mean managing the OS, scaling and patching yourself. Cloud Run takes the existing image as it is.
A Cloud Run function for an hour-long batch job
Cloud Run jobs (run to completion) or a batch service
Event-driven functions have short time limits. Cloud Run jobs are built to run a task to completion.
App Engine as the first choice for new container workloads
Cloud Run, the newer and more flexible serverless option
App Engine still works, but Cloud Run accepts any container, has more features and is where Google points new workloads.
GKE Autopilot when you need to SSH into nodes or install node agents
GKE Standard
Autopilot locks down nodes: no SSH and no custom node agents. Standard mode gives node-level access.

lessons.title: Choosing Storage and Databases
lessons.tests: matching data shape, scale and consistency to Cloud SQL, Spanner, AlloyDB, Firestore, Bigtable, BigQuery, Memorystore or Cloud Storage.
rules: Relational and regional, up to a few TB: Cloud SQL. Relational, global, horizontal writes, 99.999%: Spanner. PostgreSQL with heavy analytics on the same data: AlloyDB.
Flexible-schema documents for web and mobile apps: Firestore. Huge time series or IoT writes with millisecond reads by key: Bigtable.
Analytics over TB to PB with SQL: BigQuery. Sub-millisecond cache or sessions: Memorystore. Files, media, backups and data lakes: Cloud Storage.
traps: Cloud SQL read replicas to scale writes
Spanner: Cloud SQL scales writes only vertically
Replicas only serve reads. Every write still goes to one primary, which can only grow vertically.
BigQuery as the backend for a transactional app
Cloud SQL, Spanner or Firestore; BigQuery is for analytics
BigQuery is built for big analytical scans, not many small, fast row updates.
Bigtable for a small (10 GB) app needing multi-row transactions
Firestore or Cloud SQL; Bigtable is for 1 TB and up, single-row transactions
Bigtable only pays off at scale and supports single-row transactions only. A small transactional app fits Firestore or Cloud SQL.
Local SSD for data that must survive a stop
Persistent Disk or Hyperdisk; Local SSD is scratch space
Local SSD data disappears when the VM stops or is deleted. Persistent disks outlive the VM.
Filestore for objects served over HTTP
Cloud Storage; Filestore is an NFS file share for VMs and GKE
Filestore is a file share that servers mount. Serving files to users over HTTP is what Cloud Storage (with CDN) is for.

lessons.title: Network Design and Hybrid Connectivity
lessons.tests: VPC layout, connecting projects and on-premises networks, and picking the load balancer.
rules: A VPC is global and its subnets are regional; use custom-mode VPCs in production, never the default network.
Projects in one organisation sharing a network: Shared VPC (one host project). Separate networks or organisations talking privately: VPC Network Peering.
On-premises link: HA VPN (99.99%, encrypted, over the internet) for low cost; Dedicated Interconnect (10 or 100 Gbps) or Partner Interconnect (lower bandwidth) for high, private throughput.
traps: VPC Peering to let a central team control the network of many projects
Shared VPC with a host project run by the network team
Peering joins networks that each team still controls. Shared VPC gives one team central control of one network used by many projects.
Classic VPN when the scenario asks for a 99.99% SLA
HA VPN with two tunnels and Cloud Router (BGP)
Classic VPN's SLA is 99.9%. Only HA VPN, with two tunnels and BGP, reaches 99.99%.
Overlapping IP ranges between on-premises and the VPC
Plan non-overlapping CIDR ranges before connecting
Routers can't tell overlapping ranges apart, so networks with the same ranges can't reach each other reliably once connected.
A network load balancer for path-based routing (/api, /login)
An Application Load Balancer (Layer 7)
Path and host rules work on HTTP (Layer 7). Network load balancers work on TCP and UDP and can't see URLs.
Interconnect with no fallback
Interconnect as primary with HA VPN (or a second Interconnect) as backup
A single link is a single point of failure. The exam expects a backup path for critical hybrid connectivity.

lessons.title: Availability, Disaster Recovery and Migration
lessons.tests: designing to an RTO and RPO, removing single points of failure, and planning a migration.
rules: RPO is how much data you can lose; RTO is how long you can be down. Both near zero means a hot standby with automatic failover, and costs the most.
Spread across zones for availability and across regions for disasters: regional MIGs, regional GKE clusters, Cloud SQL HA, multi-region storage.
Migrate in four phases: assess, plan the foundation (hierarchy, IAM, network), deploy, optimise. Move low-risk, low-dependency apps first.
traps: Cloud SQL read replicas to raise availability
Cloud SQL HA configuration (regional standby with automatic failover)
Cloud SQL read replicas are not promoted automatically. The HA standby is what fails over on its own.
Daily snapshots for an RPO of minutes
Continuous replication or a hot or warm standby
A daily snapshot can lose up to a day of data. An RPO of minutes needs continuous replication.
Refactor everything during the migration
Rehost or replatform first, then modernise; refactoring is the slowest and dearest
Refactoring during the move adds time and risk. Move first, then modernise once the workload runs in the cloud.
A DR plan written once and filed
Test the DR plan regularly with game days
An untested plan often fails when it's needed. Regular drills prove you can meet the RTO and RPO.
Transfer 50 TB over a slow link that would take weeks
Transfer Appliance (over about 20 TB or more than a week online)
Over a slow link the copy would take weeks and saturate the line. A shipped appliance is faster for large data.

lessons.title: Choosing AI and ML Services
lessons.tests: picking the lightest AI option that meets the need: pre-trained APIs, foundation models, tuning, AutoML or custom training.
rules: Standard task (vision, speech, translation, sentiment) with no customisation: a pre-trained API.
Chat, summarisation or generation: a foundation model such as Gemini from Model Garden in Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (formerly Vertex AI). Your own tone or domain terms: tune it.
Custom labels but no ML engineers: AutoML. Data scientists with TensorFlow or PyTorch code: custom training. Answers grounded in your documents: Agent Search or the RAG Engine.
traps: Train a custom model to detect sentiment in reviews
The Natural Language API
Sentiment is a standard task the Natural Language API already does, with no data or training needed.
Fine-tune a model so it can answer from today's product manuals
Ground it with RAG or Agent Search; tuning teaches style, not fresh facts
Tuning changes how a model writes, and facts learned that way go stale. Grounding fetches the current documents at answer time.
Custom training for a team with no ML expertise
AutoML
Custom training needs ML engineers writing code. AutoML trains from labelled data without code.
Google AI Studio for a governed enterprise deployment
Agent Studio in Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform
AI Studio is for quick experiments with a personal account. Agent Studio adds enterprise access control, security and deployment.
Build an ML model outside the warehouse when the data is in BigQuery and the team knows SQL
BigQuery ML
Moving data out adds pipelines and risk. BigQuery ML trains where the data lives, in SQL the team already knows.

domains.title: Managing and Provisioning Infrastructure
domains.sub: Configure and run what you designed: VMs and instance groups, GKE clusters, storage, data, and the resource hierarchy.

lessons.title: Compute Engine in Practice
lessons.tests: instance templates, managed instance groups, machine choice and the VM features that keep costs and boot times down.
rules: Managed instance groups (MIGs) give autoscaling, autohealing with health checks and rolling updates; regional MIGs spread VMs across zones.
Instance templates cannot be edited: copy one and change the copy. Bake software into a custom image rather than installing it in a startup script.
Fault-tolerant batch work: Spot VMs (60 to 91% off, 30 seconds' notice). Steady load: committed use discounts. Licensing or compliance needing dedicated hosts: sole-tenant nodes.
traps: Unmanaged instance group for an autoscaling web tier
A managed instance group built from an instance template
Unmanaged groups can't autoscale, autoheal or roll out updates. Only managed instance groups do.
Edit the live instance template
Create a new template and roll it out to the MIG
Instance templates can't be changed after creation. You make a new one and roll it out.
Long startup scripts to install software on every boot
A hardened custom image with the software pre-installed
Installing software at every boot slows scaling and can fail. A pre-built image starts ready to serve.
Spot VMs for a critical, always-on database
Standard VMs, with committed use discounts for the steady load
Spot VMs can be stopped at any time with 30 seconds' notice, which a critical database can't survive.
Keep a static IP reserved but unused to save money
Release it: you are billed for reserved static IPs that are not in use
A reserved static IP that isn't attached to anything is still billed. Releasing it stops the charge.

lessons.title: Running GKE
lessons.tests: node pools, cluster types, the three autoscalers, probes and disruption budgets.
rules: Regional clusters replicate the control plane across zones; Autopilot clusters are always regional. Use node pools to give each workload the right machine (GPU, high-memory, Spot).
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler adds Pods, Vertical Pod Autoscaler resizes their requests, cluster autoscaler adds and removes nodes. Spiky traffic needs HPA plus cluster autoscaler.
Startup probe for slow starters, readiness probe before sending traffic, liveness probe to restart a stuck container. PodDisruptionBudget keeps Pods up during maintenance.
traps: Zonal cluster for a production app that must survive a zone outage
Regional cluster
A zonal cluster's control plane lives in one zone. A regional cluster keeps running when a zone fails.
One big node pool for GPU and web workloads
A separate GPU node pool, with nodeSelector or taints
Mixing workloads wastes expensive GPU nodes on ordinary Pods. A separate pool lets only GPU work land there.
Liveness probe to stop traffic until the database is ready
Readiness probe
A failing liveness probe restarts the container. A readiness probe just holds traffic back until the app is ready.
Pods stuck in Pending: restart them
Not enough capacity: let cluster autoscaler add nodes or lower the requests
Pending means the scheduler can't find room. Restarting adds no capacity; more nodes or smaller requests do.
ImagePullBackOff fixed by adding more nodes
Check the image name and tag, and that the node service account can read Artifact Registry
The node can't fetch the image, so more nodes would fail the same way. Fix the name, the tag or the registry permission.

lessons.title: Storage and Data Operations
lessons.tests: snapshots and images, Cloud Storage lifecycle and retention, data transfer and BigQuery table design.
rules: Snapshots are incremental and can be scheduled with automatic deletion. A machine image copies a whole VM (config plus all disks); a custom image copies one boot disk.
Lifecycle rules move objects to Nearline (30 days minimum), Coldline (90) or Archive (365) and delete them later. A locked retention policy makes objects undeletable until they age out.
Under 1 TB: `gcloud storage cp`. Over 1 TB, or from another cloud, on a schedule: Storage Transfer Service. Very large or slow link: Transfer Appliance.
traps: Back up a VM's config and every attached disk with disk snapshots
A machine image
Snapshots copy disks only. A machine image also captures the VM's configuration and all its disks together.
Keep logs for 4 years in Standard storage
Lifecycle rule to Archive after 30 days, delete after 4 years
Standard is the most expensive class for data nobody reads. Lifecycle rules move it to cheaper classes automatically.
Object versioning to meet a write-once compliance rule
A locked retention policy (Bucket Lock)
Versioning keeps old copies, but anyone with rights can still delete them. A locked retention policy can't be bypassed, even by admins.
`gsutil` for 3 TB from Azure Blob Storage
Storage Transfer Service
Command-line copies don't schedule, resume or verify well for large cross-cloud moves. Storage Transfer Service does.
Scan a full BigQuery table to filter by date
Partition by the date column, cluster by the common filter, and check with a dry run
BigQuery bills the data a query scans. Partitioning lets a date filter read only the matching partitions.

lessons.title: Resource Hierarchy, Billing and Network Operations
lessons.tests: organising projects, controlling spend and configuring firewall rules and private access.
rules: Organization, then folders (per department), then projects (one per app per environment), then resources. Policies inherit downward.
Billing budgets alert at thresholds (50, 90, 100% by default); they do not stop spending. Export billing to BigQuery to analyse it.
Firewall rules are stateful; the lowest number has the highest priority. Default rules allow all egress and deny all ingress. Load balancer health checks come from 130.211.0.0/22 and 35.191.0.0/16.
traps: Dev and prod in one project, separated by labels
Separate projects per environment
Projects are the main boundary for IAM, quotas and billing. Labels don't stop a dev mistake from hitting production.
A budget alert to cap spending
Budgets only notify; automate a response through Pub/Sub if you must act
Budgets send alerts only. Spending carries on unless you build an automated action.
Health checks fail: make the VMs public
Allow ingress from the health check ranges in the firewall
Health checks come from Google's fixed ranges. Allowing just those keeps the VMs private.
Give private VMs external IPs so they can reach Google APIs
Enable Private Google Access on the subnet
Private Google Access lets internal-only VMs reach Google APIs without exposing them to the internet.
External IPs on private VMs so they can download updates
Cloud NAT with Cloud Router
Cloud NAT gives outbound internet access while nothing can connect in.

domains.title: Designing for Security and Compliance
domains.sub: Identity and access, service accounts, data protection, network and workload security, and meeting regulations.

lessons.title: IAM, Identity and Organisation Policy
lessons.tests: who gets which role at which level, and the difference between IAM and organisation policies.
rules: Grant predefined roles to groups, at the lowest level that works. Basic roles (Owner, Editor, Viewer) are too broad for production.
The effective policy is the union of a resource's policy and every parent's; a grant higher up cannot be taken away lower down (use deny policies if you must).
IAM decides who can do what. Organisation policies decide what can exist (allowed regions, no external IPs, no service account keys) whoever asks.
traps: Grant roles to each person one by one
Grant roles to a Google group
Group grants are easier to audit and to update as people join and leave.
Remove access in a project that was granted at the folder
Remove it at the folder, or use an IAM deny policy
Allow policies are inherited and add up. A lower level can't remove a higher grant, except with a deny policy.
IAM to stop anyone creating resources outside the EU
An organisation policy restricting resource locations
IAM controls who can act. An organisation policy limits what can be created, whoever tries.
Editor role for a developer who only deploys
The narrow predefined role (or a custom role) for that job
Editor can change almost everything in the project. Least privilege means the narrowest role that does the job.
Cloud IAM for your app's customer sign-in
Identity Platform; IAM is for employees and workloads
IAM is for people and workloads that manage Google Cloud. Your app's end users sign in through Identity Platform.

lessons.title: Service Accounts and Workload Identity
lessons.tests: how code authenticates without long-lived keys, on Google Cloud, in GKE and from outside.
rules: Code on Google Cloud uses an attached service account; Google rotates its credentials, so there are no keys to store.

GKE Pods needing different permissions: Workload Identity Federation for GKE, one Kubernetes service account per microservice. Common permissions for all Pods (logging, monitoring): the node service account.
Workloads outside Google Cloud (AWS, Azure, on-premises with an IdP): Workload Identity Federation with short-lived tokens. Downloaded keys are the last resort.
traps: Download a service account key for an app on a VM
Attach a service account to the VM
Key files can leak and must be rotated by hand. An attached service account gets short-lived credentials automatically.
Use the default Compute Engine service account with Editor
A user-managed service account per app with only the roles it needs
The default account often has broad Editor rights. A dedicated account limits the damage if the app is compromised.
Give every Pod the node's broad service account
Workload Identity Federation for GKE per microservice
Every Pod on the node would share the same permissions. Workload Identity gives each workload only its own.
Store a key file in the repo for a GitHub Actions deploy
Workload Identity Federation from GitHub's OIDC tokens
A stored key is a long-lived secret. Federation swaps the CI system's own token for short-lived Google credentials.
Grant the role in Project A so its VM can read a bucket in Project B
Grant the VM's service account the role on the bucket in Project B
Access is granted on the resource being used. The bucket lives in Project B, so the grant goes there.

lessons.title: Protecting Data
lessons.tests: encryption key options, secrets, sensitive data and preventing data from leaving a perimeter.
rules: Everything is encrypted at rest by default. Need to control or rotate the key: customer-managed keys (CMEK) in Cloud KMS. Must hold the key yourself: customer-supplied keys (CSEK), sent with each request.
Passwords and API keys go in Secret Manager (versioned, audited), never in code or environment files in the image.
Find and mask PII: Sensitive Data Protection (Cloud DLP). Stop data being copied out of a set of projects even by a valid identity: VPC Service Controls.
traps: CSEK when the scenario only asks to manage and rotate keys
CMEK in Cloud KMS
With CSEK you supply and guard the key on every request. CMEK gives control and rotation with far less work.
Hard-code the database password in the container
Secret Manager, read at runtime by the service account
Passwords baked into images leak through registries and logs and are hard to rotate. Secret Manager keeps them separate and audited.
IAM alone to stop an insider copying BigQuery data to a personal project
A VPC Service Controls perimeter
A user who is allowed to read can still copy data out. A service perimeter blocks data leaving the boundary.
Make a bucket public so a partner can download one file
A signed URL with a short expiry
A public bucket exposes everything in it. A signed URL shares one object for a limited time.
Store raw PII in BigQuery and restrict the table
De-identify with Sensitive Data Protection before loading
A restricted table still holds raw PII that can leak. De-identifying first lowers the risk and keeps the data useful.

lessons.title: Network, Workload Security and Compliance
lessons.tests: Cloud Armor, IAP, private clusters, supply-chain controls, audit logs and regulated workloads.
rules: Cloud Armor on an external Application Load Balancer blocks DDoS, OWASP Top 10 attacks and IP or geo ranges. Identity-Aware Proxy gives users access to internal apps without a VPN.
GKE hardening: private nodes plus Cloud NAT, authorised networks for the control plane, default-deny NetworkPolicies, Binary Authorization for signed images, GKE Sandbox for untrusted code.
Compliance is shared: sign a BAA for HIPAA, isolate the PCI environment in its own project, keep audit logs in a locked bucket, and use only covered services.
traps: A VPN for staff to reach an internal web app
Identity-Aware Proxy
A VPN opens up the network. IAP grants access to just that app, based on identity and context.
Firewall rules to stop SQL injection
Cloud Armor WAF rules on the load balancer
Firewall rules filter IPs and ports, not request content. A web application firewall inspects HTTP requests for attacks.
Trust any image from the registry in production
Binary Authorization: only signed, attested images deploy
Without attestation, anyone who can push an image can run it. Binary Authorization only allows signed, approved images.
Run untrusted third-party code in a normal node pool
A node pool with GKE Sandbox
An escape from a container could reach the node and other workloads. GKE Sandbox adds an extra isolation layer.
Assume Google is responsible for HIPAA compliance
Sign the BAA and configure your own controls; it is shared
Google secures the platform, but you must sign a BAA and configure your own workloads to comply.

domains.title: Analysing and Optimising Technical and Business Processes
domains.sub: Cost control, data pipelines, and the people side: stakeholders, change, continuity and SRE.

lessons.title: Optimising Cost
lessons.tests: which lever cuts cost for a workload without breaking a requirement.
rules: Steady, predictable load: committed use discounts (1 or 3 years). Interruptible work: Spot VMs. Variable load: autoscaling, or serverless that scales to zero.
GKE Autopilot bills Pod requests, not whole nodes; set requests carefully. Cloud Run request-based billing suits spiky traffic, instance-based suits steady traffic.
BigQuery bills data scanned: partition and cluster tables, avoid `SELECT *`, dry-run queries, batch-load instead of streaming, and let unused tables expire.
traps: Committed use discounts for a two-week experiment
On-demand or Spot VMs
Commitments last 1 or 3 years. You'd pay for a year to use two weeks.
Bigger VMs to fix a slow, rarely used internal tool
Right-size from recommendations, or move it to serverless
Over-sizing raises cost without fixing the real need. Right-sizing or serverless matches spend to actual use.
Streaming inserts for a nightly file load into BigQuery
Batch load jobs, which are free
Streaming inserts cost money and suit real-time needs. Nightly files load free as batch jobs.
Keep all data in Standard storage for simplicity
Lifecycle rules to colder classes as access drops
Paying Standard rates for data nobody reads wastes money. Lifecycle rules move it to cheaper classes.
Guess where money goes
Export billing to BigQuery and analyse it in Looker Studio
The billing export gives line-level cost by project, service and label, so you can see where money really goes.

lessons.title: Data Pipelines and Analytics
lessons.tests: building ingest, process, store and analyse pipelines with the right managed service at each step.
rules: Streaming ingest: Pub/Sub. Batch ingest: Storage Transfer Service, BigQuery Data Transfer Service or Transfer Appliance.
New batch or streaming pipelines with no cluster: Dataflow (Apache Beam). Existing Spark or Hadoop jobs: Dataproc. Visual cleaning for analysts: Dataprep. Orchestration: Cloud Composer.
Ad hoc SQL analytics: BigQuery. Fixed, high-throughput time-series lookups: Bigtable. Dashboards: Looker or Looker Studio.
traps: Dataproc for a brand new streaming pipeline
Dataflow
Dataproc means running Spark clusters. Dataflow is serverless and built for new batch and streaming pipelines.
Rewrite existing Spark jobs in Beam to move them
Run them on Dataproc first
Rewriting delays the migration and adds risk. Dataproc runs existing Spark jobs with few changes.
Call the warehouse directly from every sensor
Pub/Sub to buffer, Dataflow to process, then BigQuery or Bigtable
Direct writes overload the store during spikes and lose data during outages. Pub/Sub buffers and Dataflow transforms.
Pub/Sub alone for exactly-once, de-duplicated processing
Pub/Sub with Dataflow (or Pub/Sub exactly-once delivery on a pull subscription)
Pub/Sub delivers at least once by default, so duplicates happen. Dataflow or exactly-once delivery removes them.
BigQuery for single-key lookups in milliseconds at millions of writes per second
Bigtable
BigQuery is optimised for large scans, not millisecond single-row lookups at huge write rates. Bigtable is.

lessons.title: Stakeholders, Change, Continuity and SRE
lessons.tests: the architect's non-technical work, and the reliability vocabulary the exam expects.
rules: SLI is the measure, SLO is the target, SLA is the contract with penalties. Keep internal SLOs stricter than the SLA. The error budget (100% minus the SLO) decides how fast you can ship.
Business continuity covers people and processes; disaster recovery is its IT part. Both need named owners, an RTO and RPO, and regular tests.
Incidents end with a blameless postmortem that asks how to stop a repeat, not who to blame. Manage change by explaining the reason, the risk and who is affected.
traps: Promise customers the same SLA as the internal SLO
Set the SLA looser than the internal SLO
If the contract equals the internal target, any slip costs money. A stricter internal SLO gives a safety margin.
Freeze all releases forever after one outage
Use the error budget: slow releases only while it is spent
Freezing stops all improvement. The error budget says when to slow down and when it's safe to ship.
Postmortem that names who caused the outage
Blameless postmortem with action items
Blame makes people hide mistakes. Blameless reviews find system fixes that prevent a repeat.
Tell stakeholders about the migration at go-live
Identify stakeholders early and plan the communication
Late surprises create resistance and missed requirements. Early communication brings buy-in and feedback.
Chase 100% availability
Pick an SLO users need; each extra nine costs far more
Each extra nine costs much more, and users often can't tell. Aim for the reliability users actually need.

domains.title: Managing Implementation
domains.sub: Ship changes safely: release strategies, CI/CD and infrastructure as code, and the tools and APIs used to build on Google Cloud.

lessons.title: Release Strategies
lessons.tests: which deployment strategy meets the release goals, and how to do it on MIGs, Cloud Run, App Engine and GKE.
rules: Rolling: gradual, no extra infrastructure. Blue/green: instant switch and rollback, needs double capacity during the release. Canary: a small slice of traffic first. Recreate: cheapest, but downtime.
Test whether users like a feature: A/B testing. Test with real production traffic and no user impact: shadow (mirrored) traffic.

Cloud Run and App Engine split traffic between revisions or versions; MIGs run rolling or canary updates with max surge and max unavailable; GKE canaries by percentage need Gateway API or a service mesh.
traps: Recreate for an app that must have zero downtime
Rolling or blue/green
Recreate stops the old version before starting the new one, so users see downtime.
Rolling update when instant rollback is the key requirement
Blue/green
Rolling back a rolling update is another slow rollout. Blue/green switches traffic back at once.
Deploy a new Cloud Run revision straight to 100%
Deploy with no traffic, then shift a percentage
Sending all traffic at once exposes every user to any bug. A small split tests the new revision first.
Kubernetes Deployment alone for a 5% traffic canary
Gateway API traffic splitting or Cloud Service Mesh
A Deployment can only approximate splits through replica counts. Gateway API or a service mesh routes exact percentages.
Rolling update with max unavailable 1 when capacity must not drop
Max surge 1, max unavailable 0
Max unavailable 1 takes an instance down before its replacement is ready. Surge 1, unavailable 0 adds the new one first.

lessons.title: CI/CD and Infrastructure as Code
lessons.tests: building a delivery pipeline and keeping infrastructure in version-controlled code.
rules: Cloud Build builds and tests, Artifact Registry stores and scans images and packages, Cloud Deploy promotes releases through environments.
Define infrastructure with Terraform (or Infrastructure Manager, which runs Terraform for you) and change it only through that code, so environments do not drift.
Keep many GKE clusters in line with Git: Config Sync (GitOps). Manage Google Cloud resources with Kubernetes YAML: Config Connector. Enforce cluster rules: Policy Controller.
traps: Container Registry for new projects
Artifact Registry
Container Registry is retired. Artifact Registry replaces it, with more formats and vulnerability scanning.
Fix a production setting by hand in the console
Change the Terraform code and apply it
Manual changes drift from the code and get overwritten on the next apply. Change the code so it stays the source of truth.
Script `kubectl apply` against each cluster in turn
Config Sync from one Git repository across the fleet
Per-cluster scripts drift and can fail halfway. Config Sync keeps every cluster matching Git automatically.
Run tests only after deploying to production
Unit, integration and security checks in the pipeline before release
Bugs found in production cost the most. Checks in the pipeline catch them before release.
Develop against live Pub/Sub, Spanner and Firestore
Use the local emulators for development
Developing against live services costs money and risks real data. Emulators run locally for free.

lessons.title: Tools, APIs and Integration
lessons.tests: the right command-line tool, decoupling services, and managing APIs.
rules: `gcloud` manages most services; `gcloud storage` (faster than `gsutil`) for Cloud Storage, `bq` for BigQuery, `cbt` for Bigtable, `kubectl` for Kubernetes objects.
Decouple producers and consumers with Pub/Sub; route Google Cloud events (a file upload, an audit log entry) to Cloud Run with Eventarc; schedule jobs with Cloud Scheduler.
Full API management (developer portal, quotas, monetisation, a facade over legacy systems): Apigee. Simple managed gateway for serverless backends: API Gateway.
traps: `gcloud` to read and write Bigtable rows
`cbt` or the client libraries
`gcloud` manages Bigtable instances, clusters and tables. Reading and writing rows uses `cbt` or the client libraries.
Synchronous calls from every service to a slow logging service
Publish to Pub/Sub and let the consumer catch up
If the logging service slows or fails, every caller slows or fails with it. A queue decouples them.
Polling a bucket for new files
An Eventarc or Cloud Storage trigger
Polling wastes calls and adds delay. An event trigger runs as soon as the file lands.
API Gateway when partners need a portal, keys and monetisation
Apigee
API Gateway has no developer portal or monetisation. Apigee is built for full API products.
Cron on a VM kept running only to trigger jobs
Cloud Scheduler
A VM kept running only for cron costs money and needs patching. Cloud Scheduler is managed and cheap.

domains.title: Ensuring Solution and Operations Excellence
domains.sub: Observe, run and troubleshoot what is in production, using Google Cloud Observability and SRE practice.

lessons.title: Monitoring, Logging and Tracing
lessons.tests: which observability tool answers the question, and where logs go and for how long.
rules: Metrics, dashboards, uptime checks and alerts: Cloud Monitoring. Logs: Cloud Logging. A slow request across services: Cloud Trace. CPU and memory hot spots in code: Cloud Profiler. Grouped exceptions: Error Reporting.
Install the Ops Agent on VMs for memory, disk and application metrics and logs. Watch the four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors and saturation.

The _Required bucket keeps admin activity and system event logs for 400 days at no cost; _Default keeps the rest for 30 days. Use the Log Router and sinks to send logs to Cloud Storage, BigQuery or Pub/Sub.
traps: Expect memory metrics from a VM with no agent
Install the Ops Agent
Without an agent, Compute Engine only sees what the hypervisor sees. Memory and disk usage need the Ops Agent.
Cloud Logging to find which microservice adds latency
Cloud Trace
Logs show events one service at a time. Trace follows a single request across services and shows where the time went.
Keep audit logs 7 years in the _Default bucket
A sink to a Cloud Storage bucket with a locked retention policy
_Default keeps logs 30 days unless changed and is not a write-once store. A locked bucket keeps them unchanged for years.
Expect data access logs to be on by default
Turn on Data Access audit logs (except BigQuery, on by default)
Data Access logs are off by default for most services because of their volume. You turn them on (BigQuery's are always on).
Let auditors browse Cloud Logging
Export to a bucket and grant them Storage Object Viewer on it
Logging access shows auditors far more than they need. An exported bucket with read-only access is scoped and cheap.

lessons.title: Reliability Engineering
lessons.tests: designing systems that degrade gracefully and proving it with testing.
rules: Retry with exponential backoff and jitter on 429 and 5xx errors; use circuit breakers so one failing service does not take down the rest.
Degrade gracefully: serve cached or static content, drop optional features, shed low-priority load, rather than fail completely.
Prove resilience with load tests that include spikes, chaos and failover tests, and DR drills. Measure MTTD, MTTR and MTBF to see if it is improving.
traps: Retry immediately in a tight loop
Exponential backoff with jitter
Instant retries pile load onto a struggling service. Backoff with jitter spreads retries out so it can recover.
Let the whole site fail when the recommendation service is down
Show a default list and keep checkout working
A non-essential feature failing shouldn't take down essential paths. Degrade the optional part and keep the core working.
Load test only with steady traffic
Include sudden spikes like the real launch
Launches and sales spike suddenly. Testing only steady load misses autoscaling and cold-start problems.
Assume the backup VPN works because it is configured
Fail over to it in a planned test
Untested failover often fails in practice. Only a real test proves the backup works.
Page the team on every warning
Alert on symptoms tied to SLOs so alerts are actionable
Too many alerts get ignored. Alerts tied to user-facing SLOs mean someone really needs to act.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting
lessons.tests: reading the symptom and going to the most likely cause first.
rules: VM will not boot or start: check quotas, a full boot disk and the serial port output; attach the disk to another VM to inspect it.
`kubectl` times out: check authorised networks for the control plane, the endpoint and your credentials (`gcloud container clusters get-credentials`).
Backends marked unhealthy behind a load balancer: check the firewall allows the health check ranges and the health check path and port are right.
traps: Recreate the VM when it hangs at boot
Read the serial port output first
Recreating throws away the clues and may repeat the fault. The serial port output shows why the boot failed.
Raise the machine size when a VM creation fails with a quota error
Request more quota or pick another region
A bigger VM needs more quota, not less. Request more quota or use a region with headroom.
Open the GKE control plane to 0.0.0.0/0 to fix `kubectl` timeouts
Add your client range (such as Cloud Shell) to authorised networks
Opening the control plane to the internet removes a key protection. Add only your client's range.
CrashLoopBackOff: add more replicas
Read `kubectl logs` and `kubectl describe pod` for the crash reason
Every new replica will crash the same way. The logs and pod events show the cause.
Cloud SQL connections from Cloud Run fail: open the database to the internet
Use the Cloud SQL connector or Auth Proxy with private IP
Opening a database to the internet invites attacks. Private IP with the connector is secure and recommended.

domains.title: The Four Case Studies
domains.sub: Questions about four fictional companies make up a big part of the exam. Know each one's environment and goals before exam day, then answer from the requirements.

lessons.title: Altostrat Media
lessons.tests: a media company with a large audio and video library that wants AI for content and engagement, while keeping costs and hybrid operations under control.
rules: Today: legacy on-premises ingest and archive, GKE for content delivery, Cloud Storage for media, BigQuery for audience analytics, Cloud Run functions for transcoding and metadata.
Hybrid GKE across sites: GKE Enterprise (fleets) with Cloud Interconnect. Long transcoding jobs: Cloud Run jobs, not functions with time limits. Storage cost: lifecycle rules to colder classes.
AI: Speech-to-Text plus Gemini for summaries and metadata, Vision and Video AI for harmful content, Conversational Agents for 24/7 support, with audit logs and explainability for every model.
traps: Bigger function timeouts for long transcodes
Cloud Run jobs
Functions have hard time limits. Long transcodes belong in Cloud Run jobs, which run to completion.
Keep the whole media library in Standard storage
Lifecycle rules to Nearline, Coldline and Archive by age
Most of a media archive is rarely played. Colder classes cut storage cost sharply, which the case asks for.
Train a custom model to summarise podcasts
Speech-to-Text, then a Gemini model to summarise
Speech-to-Text and Gemini already transcribe and summarise. Custom training is slower and costlier.
Manage on-premises and cloud clusters separately
One fleet with GKE Enterprise and Config Sync
The case asks for consistent hybrid operations. One fleet applies the same configuration and policy everywhere.
Email alerts from separate tools
Google Cloud Observability with alerting policies
The case wants unified reliability. One observability suite gives one view and consistent alerting.

lessons.title: Cymbal Retail
lessons.tests: a fast-growing online retailer with manual catalogue work, data silos and a costly call centre.
rules: Catalogue enrichment: Gemini and Imagen models on Agent Platform generate attributes, descriptions and image variants from supplier data, with a human-in-the-loop review app (for example on Cloud Run).
Discovery: Agent Search for natural-language product search and Discovery AI for recommendations. Support: Conversational Agents and Agent Assist to cut call-centre cost.
Modernise: MySQL and SQL Server to Cloud SQL or AlloyDB, Redis to Memorystore, Kubernetes workloads to GKE or Cloud Run, Pub/Sub, Dataflow and BigQuery to break the silos.
traps: Publish AI-generated product text straight to the site
A human review step before publishing
The case requires human-in-the-loop review, because AI-generated content can be wrong or off-brand.
Build a search engine on a VM with open-source tools
A managed Google search and recommendations service
A managed search and recommendations service is faster to deliver and keeps improving. A self-built one adds operations work.
Hire more agents for growing call volume
Conversational Agents for routine calls, Agent Assist for the rest
The case wants lower call-centre costs. Virtual agents take routine calls and Agent Assist speeds up the rest.
Keep each tool's monitoring (Grafana, Nagios, Elastic)
Consolidate on Google Cloud Observability
Separate tools fragment monitoring. The case asks for proactive, unified monitoring.
Move the catalogue databases to BigQuery
Cloud SQL, AlloyDB or Spanner for transactions; BigQuery for analytics
Catalogue and orders are transactional data. BigQuery is the analytics layer, not the operational store.

lessons.title: EHR Healthcare
lessons.tests: an electronic health records SaaS provider leaving colocation facilities, needing 99.9% uptime, compliance and faster releases.
rules: Containerised apps on Kubernetes: GKE, managed as one fleet with GKE Enterprise and Config Sync for consistent environments and CI/CD from Git.
Databases: MySQL and SQL Server to Cloud SQL (or AlloyDB or Spanner), Redis to Memorystore, MongoDB to MongoDB Atlas. Legacy insurer integrations stay on-premises over Dedicated Interconnect.

Identity: keep Active Directory, sync with Google Cloud Directory Sync and sign in with SSO. Health data: a BAA, audit logs retained in Cloud Storage and analysed in BigQuery, and alerts that people act on.
traps: Move the legacy insurer interfaces to Google Cloud now
Leave them on-premises and connect over Interconnect; they are being replaced
The case says these interfaces are being replaced and are not moving. Keep them on-premises and connect privately.
Create new Google accounts for every employee
Federate with Active Directory (GCDS plus SSO)
They already run Active Directory. Sync plus SSO keeps one identity source and one password per person.
Classic VPN for a secure high-speed link
Dedicated Interconnect
The case asks for a secure, high-speed link. Interconnect gives dedicated bandwidth and a higher SLA.
Run each environment's clusters by hand
GKE Enterprise fleet with Config Sync
Their outages came from misconfiguration. Git-driven configuration across a fleet removes manual drift.
More open-source monitoring tools
Cloud Monitoring alerting policies and Cloud Logging with retention
Their problem is ignored alerts, not missing tools. Actionable alerting policies and retained logs fix it.

lessons.title: KnightMotives Automotive
lessons.tests: a car maker modernising mainframes and dealer systems, adding AI to vehicles and building a data platform under EU data law.
rules: In the car: Android Automotive OS, Dialogflow voice assistants and Edge TPUs for real-time models on the vehicle. Simulation and autonomy training: GPUs and TPUs (AI Hypercomputer).
Data: Pub/Sub and Dataflow for vehicle telemetry, BigQuery as the single platform to end silos and monetise data, Sensitive Data Protection to anonymise personal data before analysis.
Legacy: Mainframe Connector and the mainframe assessment tool, Gemini Code Assist to help rewrite code, then GKE or Cloud Run; expose dealer and partner data through Apigee.
traps: Send every sensor reading to the cloud before the car decides
Run the model on the vehicle with Edge TPUs
A car can't wait for a round trip or rely on rural coverage. Decisions must run on the vehicle.
Rewrite the mainframe in one big project
Assess, connect, then move and rewrite in stages
Big-bang rewrites are high risk. Assess, connect and move in stages so the business keeps running.
Load identifiable driver data straight into BigQuery
Anonymise it with Sensitive Data Protection first
EU data law and data monetisation both require personal data to be protected. Anonymise it before analysts see it.
One region outside the EU for all data
Keep EU data in EU regions with location policies
EU rules may require EU residency. Location policies keep data in approved regions.
Give dealers database access for orders
Secure APIs through Apigee or API Gateway
Direct database access is insecure and tightly coupled. APIs give controlled, monitored access.

domains.title: Compute Services
domains.sub: Where code runs, from full virtual machines to serverless containers and functions, and how to choose.

lessons.title: Compute Engine
lessons.what: Virtual machines on Google's infrastructure (IaaS). You choose the machine, the OS and the software, and you run it.
lessons.tests: when a workload needs full control of the OS, specific licences or hardware, or a lift-and-shift with no changes.
rules: Machine families: general purpose (E2, N2, N4) for most work, compute-optimised (C-series) for CPU-heavy work, memory-optimised (M-series) for big in-memory databases, accelerator-optimised (A and G series) for GPUs.
Billed per second after the first minute. A stopped VM costs nothing for compute, but its disks and any reserved static IPs are still billed.

Save with sustained use discounts (automatic), committed use discounts (1 or 3 years) and Spot VMs (up to 91% off, can be stopped at any time). Live migration keeps VMs running through host maintenance.
traps: A VM for a stateless container web API
Cloud Run
A VM means OS, scaling and patching work. Cloud Run runs the same container with none of it.
A stopped VM costs nothing
Disks and reserved static IPs are still billed
Only compute stops billing when a VM stops. Disks and reserved IPs keep charging.
SSH keys pasted into metadata for a large team
OS Login, with access granted to IAM groups
Keys in metadata don't follow people joining or leaving. OS Login ties SSH to IAM, so removing access is instant.

lessons.title: App Engine
lessons.what: Google's original platform as a service: deploy code, and Google runs, scales and patches it. One App Engine app per project.
lessons.tests: when the scenario already uses App Engine, or asks for traffic splitting between versions of a simple web app.
rules: Standard environment: language sandboxes, starts in seconds, scales to zero. Flexible environment: Docker containers on VMs, at least one instance, SSH allowed.
An app has services (microservices), each with versions; split traffic between versions for canary or A/B tests, and deploy with `--no-promote` to release without traffic.
Scaling types: automatic (by CPU, throughput or concurrent requests), basic (instances start on request and stop when idle) and manual (a fixed count).
traps: Move an App Engine app to another region
Not possible; the region is fixed, so create a new project
An App Engine app's region is set once, at creation, and can't change.
App Engine Flexible to scale to zero
Standard environment, or Cloud Run
Flexible runs on VMs and keeps at least one instance. Standard scales to zero.
App Engine as the default for new container workloads
Cloud Run
Cloud Run is the newer, more flexible option for containers and is where Google points new workloads.

lessons.title: Cloud Run
lessons.what: Serverless containers built on Knative. Hand over a container image or source code; Google runs, scales and secures it, down to zero.
lessons.tests: when the scenario has containers, unpredictable traffic, minimal operations or pay-per-use, and no need for Kubernetes features.
rules: Four shapes: services (web apps and APIs), jobs (run to completion, scheduled with Cloud Scheduler), worker pools (pull from queues, no endpoint) and functions (event handlers).
Each deploy creates a revision; split traffic between revisions and roll back instantly. Concurrency defaults to 80 requests per instance; minimum instances avoid cold starts.

Request-based billing suits spiky traffic; instance-based billing suits steady traffic, GPUs and background threads. For global users, deploy to several regions behind a global Application Load Balancer with serverless NEGs.
traps: Set concurrency to 1 for a thread-safe app
Keep it high: fewer instances, lower cost
With concurrency 1 every request needs its own instance, which multiplies cost. Thread-safe code can share instances.
Cold starts are unavoidable on Cloud Run
Set minimum instances
Minimum instances keep warm instances ready, at some extra cost.
A GKE cluster to run one containerised API cheaply
Cloud Run, with no cluster to manage
A cluster is overhead for one service. Cloud Run gives the same container with no cluster.

lessons.title: Cloud Run functions
lessons.what: Event-driven functions (formerly Cloud Functions). Write one function; it runs when an event or HTTP request arrives. The current generation runs on Cloud Run and Eventarc.
lessons.tests: when small, single-purpose code should react to an event: a file upload, a Pub/Sub message or a database change.
rules: Triggers: HTTP, Pub/Sub, Cloud Storage and 90+ event types through Eventarc, including Cloud Audit Logs entries.
An instance can serve many requests at once (up to 1,000 concurrent); HTTP functions can run up to 60 minutes, event-driven ones up to 9.
Give each function its own service account with only the roles it needs, read secrets from Secret Manager, and set minimum instances if cold starts matter.
traps: A function for an hour-long video transcode
Cloud Run jobs
Event-driven functions stop after 9 minutes. Cloud Run jobs run to completion.
Poll a bucket every minute for new files
A Cloud Storage trigger
Triggers react at once and cost nothing while idle; polling wastes calls and adds delay.
Use the default service account for every function
A dedicated, least-privilege service account per function
Separate accounts limit what a compromised function can reach.

lessons.title: Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)
lessons.what: Managed Kubernetes. Google runs the control plane; you run workloads. Autopilot mode also manages the nodes.
lessons.tests: when the scenario needs Kubernetes: many microservices, portability, existing Kubernetes skills, custom networking or hybrid clusters.
rules: Autopilot: Google manages nodes, billing is per Pod request, always regional. Standard: you manage node pools, pay per node, and can use GPUs, Spot VMs and node access.
Production clusters: regional, private nodes with Cloud NAT, Workload Identity, a release channel (Stable for production), Shielded Nodes and Binary Authorization.
Expose services with Ingress or the Gateway API (one load balancer for many services) rather than one LoadBalancer Service each. `gcloud` manages clusters; `kubectl` manages objects inside them.
traps: `kubectl` to create a cluster
`gcloud container clusters create`; `kubectl` works inside it
`kubectl` talks to an existing cluster's API. The cluster itself is a Google Cloud resource created with `gcloud` or Terraform.
A LoadBalancer Service for each of 20 microservices
One Ingress or Gateway with path or host rules
Each LoadBalancer Service creates its own load balancer and IP, which multiplies cost. Ingress or Gateway shares one.
Autopilot bills for whole nodes
Autopilot bills Pod CPU and memory requests
In Autopilot you pay for what Pods request, so unused node capacity isn't billed.

domains.title: Storage Services
domains.sub: Object, block and file storage, and the tools that move data into Google Cloud.

lessons.title: Cloud Storage
lessons.what: Object storage for any amount of unstructured data: files, media, backups, logs and data lakes. 99.999999999% (11 nines) annual durability.
lessons.tests: when data is files or blobs, needs cheap durable storage, a data lake, static website hosting, or a landing zone for transfers.
rules: Storage classes by access: Standard (no minimum), Nearline (30 days, about once a month), Coldline (90 days, once a quarter), Archive (365 days, once a year). Colder is cheaper to store but costs to read. Autoclass moves objects for you.
Locations: region (lowest cost, data next to compute), dual-region or multi-region (higher availability, geo-redundant). Bucket names are global; objects can be up to 5 TiB.
Control access with uniform bucket-level access and IAM; give temporary access with signed URLs; protect data with versioning, lifecycle rules and locked retention policies.
traps: Archive for data read every month
Nearline; Archive's retrieval fees and 365-day minimum would cost more
Archive charges more per read and bills a 365-day minimum, so monthly reads cost more than Nearline.
Object ACLs to manage access to a whole bucket
Uniform bucket-level access with IAM
ACLs are per object and hard to audit. Uniform access applies IAM to the whole bucket.
Multi-region for a batch job that runs in one region
A regional bucket in the same region
Multi-region costs more and adds nothing when compute is in one region. Regional is cheaper and closer.

lessons.title: Persistent Disk, Hyperdisk and Local SSD
lessons.what: Block storage for VMs. Persistent Disk and Hyperdisk are network disks that outlive the VM; Local SSD is physically attached and temporary.
lessons.tests: which disk fits a VM's performance, durability and cost needs.
rules: Persistent Disk types: standard (HDD, cheap, sequential), balanced (general SSD) and SSD (high IOPS). Hyperdisk lets you set IOPS and throughput separately from size.
Regional Persistent Disk replicates synchronously across two zones for fast failover. Disks can grow while attached; snapshots are incremental and can be scheduled.
Local SSD gives the highest IOPS and lowest latency but data is lost when the VM stops; use it for caches and scratch data only.
traps: Local SSD for a database's only copy of data
Persistent Disk or Hyperdisk
Local SSD data is lost when the VM stops. A database needs durable disks.
Zonal disk when a VM must recover in another zone with no data loss
Regional Persistent Disk
A zonal disk lives in one zone. A regional disk keeps a synchronous copy in a second zone.
A bigger VM to get more disk IOPS
A larger disk, a faster disk type or Hyperdisk with provisioned IOPS
Disk performance depends mostly on disk type and size (or provisioned IOPS), not on the VM alone.
